text: GPGPU is {{c1::heterogeneous}} computing: a host {{c2::CPU}} runs the main program, and kernels run on the {{c3::GPU}}.
extra: The host loads data and kernels, copies the stream to the device, launches, then copies results back.

text: CPU and GPU usually keep {{c1::separate}} memory. Moving data to the GPU means an expensive bus {{c2::copy}}, and that cost can {{c3::dominate}} a small problem.
extra: A naive GPU port can lose to CPU code when transfer time outweighs the compute you save.

text: For Warp or GPGPU work, prefer {{c1::flat, contiguous}} buffers, {{c2::uniform}} work per thread, and enough work to amortize host-device copies.
extra: Divergent branches and scattered layouts hurt lockstep GPU threads. Tiny problems die on transfer cost.

text: A function marked {{c1::@wp.kernel}} is {{c2::statically typed}}. GPU kernels {{c3::do not return}} values. They write into arrays instead.
extra: Write the body for one element. Warp launches one thread per stream element.

text: Inside a Warp kernel, {{c1::wp.tid()}} gives your per-thread {{c2::element index}}, so you can write \(z[\text{tid}] = x[\text{tid}] + y[\text{tid}]\).
extra: Same role as a thread ID or MPI rank for owning one array slot.

text: Practice: launch over \(N\) elements on an Nvidia GPU with the kernel, {{c1::dim=N}}, arguments in {{c2::inputs=}} (in order), and {{c3::device="cuda"}}.
extra: Study-guide practice Q3 answer C. device is optional and defaults to Warp's default. The lecture demo also passes outputs=[z].

text: Warp device="cpu" runs {{c1::single-thread serial}} code for portability. device="cuda" runs {{c2::in parallel}} on Nvidia GPUs.
extra: Same code and semantics on both backends. CPU mode teaches the API but gives no GPU speedup.

text: Host prep: wrap NumPy with {{c1::wp.array(...)}}, allocate the output with {{c2::wp.zeros}}, and after launch call {{c3::.numpy()}} to bring results back.
extra: Match dtype and device. For a 1D map, lengths must match. A zero array shaped like an input works too.

text: Memory models: Pthreads use a {{c1::shared}} address space. MPI uses {{c2::message passing}}. Warp keeps {{c3::separate host/device}} memory and needs explicit copies.
extra: Once data is on the GPU, kernels operate on device memory.

text: Warp fits large {{c1::data-parallel maps}} with uniform work. Pitfalls: excessive {{c2::host-device copies}} and {{c3::non-contiguous}} data.
extra: Also skip problems that are too small to amortize the transfers.

text: Inside a kernel, your output may depend only on inputs, not on {{c1::another thread's output}}. That independence maps the work onto data-parallel hardware.
extra: You can read any input element. You write one output slot.

text: In addArrays, pass typed arrays \(x\), \(y\), and output \(z\) as kernel arguments, store the sum in {{c1::z[tid]}}, and never {{c2::return}} the result.
extra: Annotate with @wp.kernel and types like wp.array(dtype=float).
